intro: The piece Pierre Boulez said brought “new breath to the art of music” begins with a single flute. Paul Paray conducts the Detroit Symphony Orchestra, recorded for Mercury in 1955.

sections.label: A · Flute alone, then the orchestra
sections.mNote: The flute’s phrase, given new harmony at each return

sections.label: B · D♭ major: the long tune
sections.mNote: Woodwinds, then strings, sing the one broad melody

sections.label: A′ · The flute again, over harp
sections.mNote: Opening tempo; harp arpeggios where there was silence

sections.label: Coda · Antique cymbals, E major
sections.mNote: The opening phrase, slower, then E major at last

cues.title: Flute, alone
cues.text: A flute, alone, marked doux et expressif. It starts on C♯, slides down to G and climbs back: a tritone, an interval that belongs to no key. Nothing sounds beneath it for three bars. Then a harp glissando, the horns, and a chord that settles nothing.
cues.evidence: Score (Fromont, 1895), bars 1–4: solo flute, Très modéré, doux et expressif; harp and horns enter in bar 4. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/4/40/IMSLP14736-Debussy_-_Pr%C3%A9lude_%C3%A0_l%27apr%C3%A8s-midi_d%27un_faune_%28orch._score%29.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: “A very free illustration”
cues.text: Debussy’s note for the first audience called the piece “a very free illustration of Mallarmé’s beautiful poem … a succession of scenes through which the desires and dreams of the faun pass in the heat of the afternoon.” Mallarmé’s faun wakes unsure whether the two nymphs he remembers were real.
cues.evidence: Debussy’s programme note for the 1894 première, quoted with the French original at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prélude_à_l'après-midi_d'un_faune; Mallarmé’s poem (1876).

cues.title: Muted strings, no trumpets
cues.text: Much of the time the strings play muted and split into many parts, a haze around the woodwinds. There are no trumpets, trombones or timpani: the only brass are four horns, and the brightest colours come from three flutes, oboes, cor anglais, clarinets and two harps.
cues.evidence: Score (Fromont, 1895): instrumentation, and string parts marked sourdines (muted) and divisés (divided).
cues.how: About the passage as a whole.

cues.title: Played twice on the first night
cues.text: At the première, in the Salle d’Harcourt on 22 December 1894, the flute solo was played by Georges Barrère, eighteen years old. The audience demanded the whole piece again, and Gustave Doret conducted it a second time.
cues.evidence: Première, venue and conductor: IMSLP work page, https://imslp.org/wiki/Prélude_à_l'après-midi_d'un_faune,_CD_87_(Debussy,_Claude). Barrère as soloist: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georges_Barrère. The encore: Boston Symphony programme note, https://www.bso.org/works/prelude-to-the-afternoon-of-a-faun

cues.title: D♭ major: the long tune
cues.text: The middle section, in D♭ major. For the first time the piece has a long, broad melody: the woodwinds sing it together over syncopated strings, then the strings take it up and carry it to the climax.
cues.evidence: Score (Fromont, 1895), bars 55–78 (from p. 15); bars 51–54 prepare the new key. Pearson Edexcel analysis of the work, https://qualifications.pearson.com/content/dam/pdf/A%20Level/Music/2013/Teaching%20and%20learning%20materials/Unit-3-5-Debussy.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Nijinsky’s faun
cues.text: In May 1912 Nijinsky made the piece into a ballet for the Ballets Russes, moving his dancers in profile like figures on a Greek vase and dancing the faun himself. Its last gesture caused a scandal: the editor of Le Figaro spiked his own critic’s review and denounced it on the front page.
cues.evidence: Première 29 May 1912, Théâtre du Châtelet; Gaston Calmette’s front-page article in Le Figaro replacing Robert Brussel’s review: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afternoon_of_a_Faun_(Nijinsky), citing Buckle, Nijinsky.

cues.title: The flute again
cues.text: Mouvement du début: the opening tempo, and the flute’s opening phrase. This time the harps ripple beneath it, where at the start there was only silence.
cues.evidence: Score (Fromont, 1895), rehearsal 8 (bar 79), p. 21: Mouvement du début, solo flute over harps and divided strings.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The conductor
cues.text: Paul Paray, conducting, won the Prix de Rome in 1911, twenty-seven years after Debussy. He ran the Detroit Symphony from 1952 and made this recording there for Mercury’s Living Presence series.
cues.evidence: Paray’s Prix de Rome (1911, cantata Yanitza) and Detroit post: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Paray. Mercury MG 50101 label: https://archive.org/details/lp_ibria-la-mer-prelude-to-the-afternoon-of_paul-paray-claude-debussy-detroit-symphony

cues.title: Antique cymbals
cues.text: The flute’s phrase once more, slower: the score asks for “more languor”. Now, for the first time, two antique cymbals sound, small tuned discs of brass struck softly, ringing E and B.
cues.evidence: Score (Fromont, 1895), rehearsal 10 (p. 27): Dans le 1er mouvement avec plus de langueur; cymbales antiques in E and B.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Mallarmé’s verdict
cues.text: Mallarmé wrote to Debussy straight from the concert: “The marvel! Your illustration of the Afternoon of a Faun, which presents no dissonance with my text, but goes much further, really, into nostalgia and into light.”
cues.evidence: Mallarmé to Debussy, December 1894; English text in Maurice Dumesnil, Claude Debussy, Master of Dreams (1940), p. 181.

cues.title: E major at last
cues.text: The piece closes in E major, the key the first tritone kept at arm’s length, and ends as quietly as it began.
cues.evidence: Score (Fromont, 1895), bars 105–110: cadence and final chord in E major.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: Into D♭ major
transitions.from: A · Flute alone, then the orchestra
transitions.to: B · D♭ major: the long tune
transitions.how: Four bars on an A♭ chord, the dominant of D♭, set up the change of key. At bar 55 the woodwinds begin the long D♭ melody together, over strings that play off the beat. The opening’s short, winding phrase is replaced by one that breathes in long spans.
transitions.evidence: Score (Fromont, 1895), bars 51–55, p. 15; Pearson Edexcel analysis, bars 51–78.

transitions.title: The opening tempo returns
transitions.from: B · D♭ major: the long tune
transitions.to: A′ · The flute again, over harp
transitions.how: The D♭ melody thins out in the strings and slows. At rehearsal 8, marked Mouvement du début, the solo flute brings back its first phrase, now over harp arpeggios and held string chords.

transitions.title: Slower, with antique cymbals
transitions.from: A′ · The flute again, over harp
transitions.how: The score returns to the first tempo “with more languor”. The flute’s phrase comes back once more, the antique cymbals enter in E and B, and the harmony starts to settle on E major.
transitions.evidence: Score (Fromont, 1895), rehearsal 10 (p. 27) to the end, bars 94–110.

composer.epithet: He trusted his ear over the rules — “pleasure is the law” — and made the piano, the flute and the orchestra sound new.
facts: Paris Conservatoire from 1872; piano with Antoine Marmontel, composition with Ernest Guiraud
Prix de Rome 1884 · Paris Exposition 1889 · Pelléas et Mélisande 1902
One completed opera, orchestral triptychs, piano collections, songs, a quartet and three late sonatas
Symbolist poetry · Mussorgsky · the Javanese gamelan · Couperin and Rameau
composer.background:
Debussy was born above his parents’ china shop in Saint-Germain-en-Laye, west of Paris, on 22 August 1862. His parents were not musicians. His father fought for the Paris Commune in 1871 and went to prison for it, and there he met Charles de Sivry, whose mother, Antoinette Mauté, taught the piano and said she had been a pupil of Chopin. She took the boy on. In 1872, aged ten, he entered the Paris Conservatoire.

His teachers could not make him out. Antoine Marmontel, his piano professor, found “a charming child, a truly artistic temperament” in January 1874; the harmony teacher Émile Durand reported in June 1879 that he was “very gifted in harmony, but hopelessly unfocused”. Years later, discussing chords at the piano with his old composition teacher Ernest Guiraud around 1890, he put his position plainly: “There is no theory. You merely have to listen. Pleasure is the law.”
